main.claim: Pick a timer, then click as fast as you can. Choose 1, 5, 10, 30 or 60 seconds, and you get your clicks per second (CPS), total clicks, a rating and a personal best saved in your browser. Free, no sign-up.

sections.heading: How the click speed test works
sections.body:
Pick a timer, then click as fast as you can until it ends. The test counts your clicks and divides the total by the time. Ten seconds with 80 clicks gives 8 clicks per second, written as 8 CPS.

1. Pick a timer: 1, 5, 10, 30 or 60 seconds.
2. Choose a mode: left mouse clicks, spacebar mode or right-click mode.
3. Click as fast as you can until the timer ends.
4. Read your total clicks, your final CPS and your rating.

Your live CPS updates while you click, so you can see your pace. Your **personal best is saved in this browser**, so the next time you open the page, you can see whether you beat it.

sections.heading: What a CPS score means
sections.body:
CPS stands for clicks per second. A higher number means more clicks in the same time. Your rating is a label for your score.

For a rough guide, RapidTables, another click test site, lists these ranges: below 4 is slow, 4 to 6 is average, 6 to 8 is good, 8 to 10 is fast, and 10 to 14 is very fast. It says most people click about 5 to 7 times per second with regular clicking.

Use these ranges as a guide, not a grade. Your finger, your mouse and the timer you pick all change the number.

sections.heading: Why the timer changes your score
sections.body:
Short runs give higher scores than long ones, and RapidTables says this is because your hand tires. A 5-second run measures a burst. A 60-second run measures how well you hold a pace.

Run the same timer three times and use the best one, or the median, so one lucky run does not decide the result. Then try a different timer to see where your speed drops off.

sections.heading: Ways people click faster
sections.body:
Regular clicking uses the index finger and is what most people do. Jitter clicking tenses the arm so the finger vibrates on the button. Butterfly clicking alternates two fingers on one button. RapidTables lists about 5 to 8 CPS for regular clicking, about 10 to 14 for jitter clicking, and up to about 20 for butterfly clicking.

These faster styles can strain your hand and wrist. Stop if you feel pain, numbness or tingling, and rest before you try again. A relaxed grip and short, daily practice is the safer way to get faster.

sections.heading: Your results stay in your browser
sections.body: Your personal best is kept in this browser, so it stays on this device. The test is free and needs no account. Use the same browser each time to keep one running record, and a different browser starts a separate one.

pages.claim: Select spacebar mode, pick a timer, and press the spacebar as fast as you can. You get your presses per second (CPS), total presses, a rating and a personal best saved in your browser. Free, in your browser, no sign-up.

sections.heading: How to run the spacebar test
sections.body:
Open the spacebar page, pick a timer, and make sure spacebar mode is selected. Then press the spacebar as fast as you can until the timer ends.

1. Open the [spacebar click speed test](https://click-speed-test.lazur.app/spacebar).
2. Pick a timer: 1, 5, 10, 30 or 60 seconds.
3. Select spacebar mode.
4. Press the spacebar as fast as you can until the timer ends.
5. Read your presses, final CPS and rating.

Start at a pace you can hold for the whole timer. A fast start can fade and cost you clicks later in the run, and the live CPS shows you when your pace drops.

sections.heading: What a spacebar score means
sections.body:
Spacebar CPS is the total presses divided by the timer, the same way as mouse CPS. KeyboardTester gives these benchmarks for one finger: an average of about 6 to 7 CPS, 8 to 10 as fast, and 3 to 5 as typical for relaxed single-finger tapping. It calls 10 to 14 competitive, which almost always needs two fingers, and says 14 and above is hard to sustain cleanly.

These numbers come from another site. Your own score is what this test shows, and your personal best is saved in this browser so you can track it from run to run. Write the timer and the final CPS in a notes file after each session, so the trend stays clear. Compare the same timer over several days rather than one busy afternoon, because your hand changes from day to day and one result proves little.

sections.heading: One finger or two
sections.body:
Most people tap the spacebar with one finger. Alternating two fingers, such as the index and middle finger, can reach higher speeds, but it takes practice. KeyboardTester suggests holding the bar with one finger while tapping with another, or bouncing between two fingers to spread the work. Try each method for a few runs and keep the one that gives you a clean, fast score.

A clean score matters. Check that a high number is not inflated by double presses. A worn switch can register one press twice, so a sudden jump in CPS is worth a second run before you believe it.

sections.heading: Warm-up and hand habits
sections.body:
Warm up with two or three short runs before you test for real. Tension slows you down, so keep your shoulder and wrist loose and tap with the finger, not the whole arm. Rest between sets, since tired fingers lose speed.

KeyboardTester recommends taking the median of three runs rather than judging by one peak. It also notes that some people find light or linear switches quicker for rapid tapping. Try the test on the keyboard you use most, because a score on a different keyboard is a separate result.

faq.q: How do I test my spacebar speed?
faq.a: Open the spacebar page, pick a timer, and press the spacebar as fast as you can until it ends. The test shows your presses, final CPS and a rating. Run it a few times and keep your best result, since one run can be off.

faq.q: How fast is a good spacebar speed?
faq.a: KeyboardTester says about 6 to 7 CPS is average for one finger, and 8 to 10 is fast. Scores of 10 to 14 almost always need two fingers, according to the same site. Use these as rough guides and compare your own best runs over time.

faq.q: Can I use two fingers on the spacebar?
faq.a: Yes. Some people hold the bar with one finger and tap with another, or alternate two fingers. Try it in a few short runs. If your hand hurts, go back to one finger and rest before you test again.

sections.heading: How to run a 1-second click test
sections.body:
Open the 1-second page, pick the 1-second timer, and click as fast as you can. The test counts the clicks you make in that one second.

1. Open the [1-second click test](https://click-speed-test.lazur.app/1-second).
2. Pick the 1-second timer.
3. Choose left-click mode, or right-click mode if you want to test the right button.
4. Click as fast as you can until the second is over.
5. Read your clicks and CPS. Your personal best is saved in this browser.

sections.heading: What a 1-second score means
sections.body:
In a 1-second run, your CPS is the number of clicks you make in that second. CPS-Check says that if your score is less than 7, you should practice for a few minutes every day. RapidTables says most people click about 5 to 7 times per second with regular clicking, and it places 14 and above in its extreme band, which it links to butterfly and drag clicking.

Those figures come from other sites. Use them to compare your number, not to judge yourself. A useful test is whether your number rises over a few weeks on the same timer. If it does, your practice is working, even if you are still below the benchmark a site lists. Small gains on one timer are a better sign than a single big score.

sections.heading: Why one second is not your whole speed
sections.body:
A 1-second run shows a burst. It does not show how long you can keep up the pace. For a fuller picture, run the same test on 10 or 30 seconds and compare.

A high 1-second score next to a low 10-second score can mean you start fast and tire quickly. Use both results to decide what to practice.

sections.heading: Tips for a better burst
sections.body:
Warm up with two or three short runs before you record a score. Keep your wrist loose and tap from the finger. Rest between sets, since tired fingers slow down. Short practice on most days works better for many people than one long session each week.

Faster techniques exist. RapidTables lists jitter clicking, which tenses the arm, at about 10 to 14 CPS, and butterfly clicking, which alternates two fingers on one button, at up to about 20 CPS. Both can strain the hand, so stop if your hand hurts.

sections.heading: Your personal best
sections.body:
Your personal best is saved in this browser, so each new run shows whether you beat it. Test the same timer in the same browser to compare like with like.

If a new run is lower than your best, that is normal. Hands are not the same from day to day, and a tired hand after a long session will score lower than a fresh one. Keep the best result as your target and try again after a rest.

faq.a: By the usual ranges, yes. RapidTables places 14 and above in its extreme band and links that speed to butterfly and drag clicking. Most people click about 5 to 7 times per second with regular clicking, so 14 is far above the typical range.

faq.q: How fast can you click in 1 second?
faq.a: Most people land between 5 and 7 clicks in one second with regular clicking, according to RapidTables. Your own number depends on your finger, your mouse and your practice. Run the 1-second test a few times and keep your best result.

faq.q: What is the average CPS in 1 second?
faq.a: RapidTables says most people click about 5 to 7 times per second with regular clicking, and that short tests score higher than long ones. Treat that as a rough guide. Your personal best in this browser is the number to track.

sections.heading: What this test counts
sections.body:
This page tests the spacebar. In spacebar mode, the test counts spacebar presses during the timer, and the CPS number is the total divided by the time. It does not test every key on the keyboard.

To check which keys respond, use the [Keyboard Test](https://keyboard-test.lazur.app/). It lights up each key while you press it and marks the keys you have already tested.

sections.heading: Reference speeds for the spacebar
sections.body:
KeyboardTester gives these benchmarks for one finger on the spacebar: about 6 to 7 CPS is average, 8 to 10 is fast, and 3 to 5 is typical for relaxed tapping. It says 10 to 14 CPS is competitive and almost always needs two fingers, and that 14 and above is hard to sustain. It cites records sitting around 12 to 15 CPS sustained over 5 seconds.

Treat these as rough guides from another site. Your own runs and your personal best show what you can do now. If your number is well below the reference, that is a starting point, not a verdict. Practice the timer you care about, keep your warm-up short, and check progress across several sessions.

sections.heading: Hand and keyboard habits
sections.body:
Warm up with two or three short runs. Keep your shoulder and wrist relaxed, and tap from the finger. Take the median of three runs instead of judging by one high peak, as KeyboardTester suggests. Check that a high score is clean, since a faulty switch can count one press twice.

KeyboardTester notes that a short actuation distance helps and that some people find light or linear switches quicker for rapid tapping. Try the test on the keyboard you use most, because a score on a different keyboard is a separate result.

sections.heading: Stay comfortable
sections.body: Rapid tapping can strain fingers and wrists. Stop if you feel pain or tingling, and rest before you test again. Your personal best is saved in this browser, so you can track progress over several days. Keep sessions short, and if your score drops sharply for several runs in a row, take a day off before you test again. A tired hand gives a different number on purpose: it shows your state that day, not your best.

faq.q: How do I test my keyboard speed?
faq.a: Open the keyboard test, pick a timer, select spacebar mode, and press the spacebar as fast as you can. The test shows your presses, final CPS and a rating. Run it a few times and keep your best result.

faq.q: Can I test keys other than the spacebar?
faq.a: This page uses spacebar mode for keyboard speed. To check which keys respond, use the Keyboard Test, which lights up each key you press. Some system keys, such as the Windows key, volume keys and Fn, never reach a web page at all.

faq.q: How fast is a good keyboard speed?
faq.a: KeyboardTester says about 6 to 7 presses per second on the spacebar with one finger is average, and 8 to 10 is fast. Two-finger tapping can reach 10 to 14. Use these as rough guides, then compare your own best runs over time.

Repeat each mode a few times before you draw a conclusion, because one run can be off. A good habit is to alternate the two modes in short blocks, so both buttons get the same warm-up and the same rest between runs. That keeps the comparison fair.

sections.heading: What your mouse score means

sections.heading: Clicking techniques

pages.title: How to Beat a Click Speed Test: Practical Tips | Lazur
pages.description: Learn how to beat a click speed test with practical steps: pick the right timer, warm up, rest, and track your personal best. Free, no sign-up.
pages.h1: How to beat click speed test
pages.claim: Set a goal on one timer, warm up, and try to beat your personal best in short runs. The test shows your CPS, total clicks and personal best, so you can see whether each change helps. Free, no sign-up.

sections.heading: Know the number you are beating
sections.body:
Your personal best is the number to beat. It is saved in this browser, so start by running one test on each timer you care about and note the result. Then aim to beat that number, one timer at a time. Do not change your technique, your mouse and your timer all at once, because you will not know which change helped. A goal on a single timer is easier to measure than a vague goal to click faster.

RapidTables gives a reference scale: below 4 is slow, 4 to 6 is average, 6 to 8 is good, 8 to 10 is fast and 10 to 14 is very fast. It says most people click about 5 to 7 times per second with regular clicking.

sections.heading: Pick the timer that matches your goal
sections.body:
A short timer, such as 1 or 5 seconds, shows burst speed. A longer timer, such as 30 or 60 seconds, shows how well you hold a pace. RapidTables notes that short tests score higher than long ones because the hand tires, so do not compare a 5-second score with a 60-second score. Pick the timer you need, practice that one, and compare it with its own best.

Is 7 clicks per second fast? By the RapidTables ranges, 7 falls in the good band, from 6 to 8. It is also at the top of the 5 to 7 range where most people click.

sections.heading: Choose a technique and build it up
sections.body: Regular clicking is the baseline. Jitter clicking, which tenses the arm, is listed at about 10 to 14 CPS, and butterfly clicking, which alternates two fingers, at up to about 20 CPS. Try one technique at a time on the same timer. A technique that raises your number but makes your clicks uneven or painful is not worth keeping.

sections.heading: Warm up, rest and log results
sections.body:
Warm up with two or three short runs before you test for real. Rest between sets, since tired fingers slow down. Take the median of three runs rather than judging by one peak, as KeyboardTester suggests for spacebar tests. Practice in short sessions most days instead of one long session each week. A warm-up of two or three runs at a relaxed pace is enough. Long, hard sessions tend to leave the hand sore, and a sore hand slows down the next day.

For a steady record, use the same browser and the same timer each time. Your personal best is saved there, so you can see whether a change helped.

sections.heading: Stop if your hand hurts
sections.body: Fast clicking can strain your fingers, wrist and forearm. Stop if you feel pain, numbness or tingling, rest, and see a doctor if it lasts. A faster number is not worth an injury.

faq.q: How can I speed up my clicking?
faq.a: Practice short runs most days, warm up before you test, and rest when your hand tires. Try one technique at a time, such as regular, jitter or butterfly clicking, and keep the one that is fast and comfortable. Track your personal best to see progress.

faq.q: Is 10 CPS with one finger good?
faq.a: RapidTables places 10 to 14 CPS in its very fast band and links jitter clicking, which tenses the arm, to that range. KeyboardTester says 10 to 14 on the spacebar almost always needs two fingers. So 10 with one finger is a fast score on those scales.
By the RapidTables ranges, 6 to 8 is good, and 8 to 10 is fast. Most people click about 5 to 7 times per second with regular clicking, so 7 is a solid score for regular clicking.

faq.q: How do I beat my own click speed record?
faq.a: Your personal best is saved in this browser. Run the same timer, warm up first, and aim for a small gain each session rather than one big jump. Compare runs on the same timer so the numbers mean something.
